text: A scoped IAM policy protects one principal. But what stops a single compromised admin, or one overly generous IAM policy, from doing damage across an entire account, or an entire organization of accounts? That's what AWS Organizations and Service Control Policies are for — guardrails that sit above IAM entirely, and they work by a rule that's easy to say and easy to get backwards.

AWS Organizations manages many accounts as one unit. The management account is the one the organization was created from — it can create or invite member accounts and apply policy across the whole structure. Organizational Units are the folders you group accounts into, commonly by environment, and OUs can nest inside each other. Attach a policy at the OU level and it reaches every account underneath it — one guardrail, set once, instead of repeated account by account.

The most common real SCP restricts which regions workloads can run in. NotAction here means every action except these, so global services like IAM and Organizations get excluded — they don't live in a region, and restricting them would break account management entirely. The Condition then denies any request made outside the approved region list. That's a deny-list SCP: it names what's forbidden and allows everything else by omission.

The other common pattern protects the controls that give you visibility in the first place: denying anyone the ability to stop CloudTrail logging, delete a GuardDuty detector, or stop the Config recorder. No condition is needed — it's an unconditional deny, attached at an OU so it reaches every account underneath, and it holds even against a role with full AdministratorAccess.

Here's the rule to actually remember: an SCP can never grant a permission. It sets the maximum permissions available — the ceiling, not the grant. The real Allow still has to come from an IAM policy inside the account. A request only succeeds when IAM and every applicable SCP both agree to allow it; either one denying is enough to block it.

SCPs cap what any IAM policy in an account can ever grant. Next lesson zooms back in on the principals themselves — IAM roles versus IAM users — and makes the case for why temporary credentials issued to a role are almost always the safer choice over a user's long-lived access keys.
